cards.title: Is the P-matrix linear complementarity problem in polynomial time?
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given n≥1, a rational P-matrix M∈Q^(n×n) and q∈Q^n, outputs rational vectors z,w≥0 satisfying w=Mz+q and zᵀw=0?
cards.definitions: A principal submatrix M[S,S] uses the same nonempty index set S⊆{1,…,n} for rows and columns. M is a P-matrix when det M[S,S]>0 for every such S. All matrix and vector entries are explicitly listed as binary signed numerators and positive denominators; N denotes their total bit length including dimensions and separators. The algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine whose running time, including output, is at most one polynomial p(N) independent of n and the entries. It must terminate within that bound on all syntactically valid rational inputs, but its output is required to satisfy the equations only when M is a P-matrix. No P-matrix recognition or certificate is supplied or required. Inequalities are coordinatewise, and zᵀw=Σ_i z_i w_i. There is no symmetry, positive-definiteness, sparsity, nondegeneracy or coefficient-size promise beyond rational encoding and the P-matrix condition. A numerical approximation alone is not an output solution.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
cards.context:
Complementarity combines linear constraints with a discrete choice: in each coordinate, at least one of z_i and w_i must vanish. For example, when M is the identity, a negative entry of q is compensated by a positive z entry, while a positive q entry remains in w. For a general matrix the coordinates interact, so the zero pattern cannot be chosen independently.

The P-matrix condition guarantees exactly one solution for every right-hand side q. This removes failure of existence and ambiguity of the answer, yet does not supply a polynomial-time method to find that answer. The distinction is a central example of total search: a mathematical existence theorem can be much easier to state than a fast algorithmic realization.

Exact rational output is meaningful in the bit model. Once a complementary zero pattern is fixed, the remaining coordinates satisfy a nonsingular rational linear system on a principal submatrix. Determinant bounds give polynomial bit length for the solution. Thus the question does not hide an unavoidable exponentially long output.

Several matrix subclasses admit polynomial algorithms. Results for tridiagonal and Hessenberg P-matrices demonstrate how additional structure can make the problem tractable. Such restrictions are absent from this card. Likewise, a polynomial iteration count involving a condition-dependent parameter does not give a polynomial bound in the full input length without a bound on that parameter.

ETH’s 2025 research report identifies general P-matrix LCP as a major unresolved optimization question and relates it to unique-sink orientations. The current target concerns solving rational LCP instances, not recognizing the P-matrix promise and not solving every abstract orientation problem. It complements the existing cards for linear programming and exact semidefinite feasibility.
cards.why: Test whether uniqueness and complementary linear structure suffice for polynomial-time exact solution of a central optimization search problem.

importance.reason: A longstanding general optimization question with a strong total-search interpretation and continuing work on both structural and algorithmic restrictions. It asks for ordinary polynomial bit complexity, distinct from strong polynomiality of LP and exact SDP feasibility.

progress.text: The P-matrix condition characterizes uniqueness of the LCP solution for every right-hand side.
Polynomial algorithms are established for tridiagonal and Hessenberg P-matrix restrictions.
ETH’s research report still lists general P-matrix LCP in polynomial time as unresolved.

cards.title: Do one-way functions imply classical key agreement?
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical two-party key-agreement protocol with negligible disagreement and computationally secret shared keys, against passive probabilistic polynomial-time eavesdroppers, in the plain public-channel model defined below?
cards.definitions: All algorithms are uniform classical probabilistic Turing machines; security parameter λ is supplied in unary. A one-way function is a deterministic polynomial-time f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* such that, for every probabilistic polynomial-time I, Pr[f(Y)=f(X) and |Y|=λ] is negligible in λ, where X is uniform in {0,1}^λ and Y is the single output of I(1^λ,f(X)); probability also includes I’s private coins. A function μ:N→[0,1] is negligible if for every integer d≥1 there is λ₀ such that μ(λ)≤λ^(−d) for all λ≥λ₀. The protocol consists of two interactive machines A,B with independent private fair coins and total worst-case computation and communication polynomial in λ. They exchange classical messages on a noiseless public channel, with no correlated initial secrets, trusted setup, random oracle or quantum communication. At termination each outputs a λ-bit string K_A,K_B. Correctness requires Pr[K_A≠K_B] to be negligible. Let T be the full public transcript, and let U_λ be an independent uniform λ-bit string. For every probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher D, |Pr[D(1^λ,T,K_A)=1]−Pr[D(1^λ,T,U_λ)=1]| must be negligible, over the honest coins, D’s coins and U_λ. The eavesdropper observes T but does not alter the messages. The target is the unrelativized existence implication; neither the construction nor its proof is required to treat f as a black box. Both premise and conclusion use the same uniform adversary convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
cards.context:
A one-way function supplies a computational asymmetry: evaluating it is easy, while recovering a preimage of a random image is hard. Key agreement asks for a different capability. Two parties begin without a common secret and exchange visible messages, yet their final common key must remain hidden from an observer. The question is whether the first kind of asymmetry always suffices for the second.

The security definition concerns the entire transcript. Merely showing that a transcript has many possible explanations is insufficient if an efficient observer can identify the common key. Likewise, keeping each party’s private randomness hidden is weaker than hiding the particular string on which both parties agree. Comparing the actual key with an independent uniform key makes the secrecy requirement explicit.

Impagliazzo and Rudich established a black-box barrier between one-way functions and key agreement. Couteau, Farshim and Mahmoody’s 2021 work studies stronger notions of black-box uselessness and proves results for specified restricted settings. Such results delimit families of constructions; they do not refute the unrestricted existence implication on this card.

The existing TCS-6545 asks for public-key encryption from one-way functions. Public-key encryption would yield a key-agreement protocol by sending a fresh random key under the published encryption key. General interactive key agreement is a separate, weaker desired primitive. A negative conclusion about a restricted encryption construction cannot by itself rule out all interactive protocols.

The classical and passive conventions matter. Quantum key distribution uses an additional communication resource, while protection against an active man-in-the-middle requires an authentication model. Neither is part of this target. The card isolates the foundational question of creating a secret by classical public interaction from the minimal generic computational assumption.
cards.why: Determine whether generic one-wayness is enough to establish a shared classical secret without prior shared randomness or setup.

importance.reason: A foundational boundary between symmetric cryptographic hardness and secret establishment through public interaction. Distinct from the existing stronger PKE-from-OWF target, and supported by a long research line on black-box barriers.

progress.text: Impagliazzo–Rudich initiate black-box separations of key agreement from one-way functions.
Black-box uselessness results address particular key-agreement settings and leave the unrestricted implication separate.

cards.title: A (1+ε)-approximation for edit distance in n^(1+o(1)) time
cards.formal: For every fixed rational ε∈(0,1), is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm A_ε that, on every pair of explicitly given strings of total length n≥2, outputs an integer D with ED(x,y)≤D≤(1+ε)ED(x,y) with probability at least 2/3, using worst-case time n^(1+o(1))?
cards.definitions: ED(x,y) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions transforming x into y, with unit cost per edit and zero cost for an equal-symbol match. String symbols are integers in {0,…,n²+1}, stored in arrays, so binary and other fixed alphabets are included. Use a word RAM with w=B_ε⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ bits for a fixed sufficiently large integer B_ε; unit-cost operations are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo 2^w and integer division by a nonzero word. Larger integers require multiple charged operations. Independent fair random bits are allowed. For each fixed ε there is one algorithm A_ε, and for every rational η>0 there are constants C_{ε,η},N_{ε,η} such that every execution on every pair of total length n≥N_{ε,η} uses at most C_{ε,η} n^(1+η) operations. A_ε halts on all inputs and has a finite worst-case bound at each smaller length as well. Constants may depend on ε and η; the algorithm may depend on ε but not on η. All preprocessing and output are charged; no advice, preprocessing oracle or input distribution is supplied. Success is required separately for every input pair. There is no additive error or promise that ED is large. Only a numerical estimate is required, not an edit script. No polynomial dependence on 1/ε or effective procedure generating A_ε from ε is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
cards.context:
Edit distance captures alignment when one sequence may have inserted or deleted symbols. The near-linear target concerns every input pair and every fixed relative tolerance. It asks whether extremely accurate estimates can be computed with an exponent approaching one, rather than merely improving on the quadratic dynamic program.

The catalogue has two related but different targets. TCS-7220 asks for a (1+ε)-approximation in n^(2−δ_ε) time, with a fixed positive exponent saving for each accuracy. TCS-6624 asks for some fixed constant-factor approximation in O(n polylog n) time. The present target strengthens the running-time requirement of the former. Its n^(1+o(1)) guarantee does not itself promise the fixed polylogarithmic overhead of the latter.

The quantifier over runtime slack is important. For a fixed accuracy ε, one algorithm must meet n^(1+η) bounds for every fixed η>0 once n is large enough. A different algorithm for each η, with uncontrolled dependence on η, is not automatically such an algorithm. Conversely, this card does not demand a common running-time bound polynomial in inverse accuracy.

Andoni and Nosatzki obtain constant-factor approximation in n^(1+η) time for each fixed η. Mao and Rubinstein’s March 2026 approximation scheme moves toward arbitrarily accurate approximation, but its stated runtime is quasi-strongly subquadratic. Those advances concern different points of the accuracy–time tradeoff and do not establish the present joint target.

Purely multiplicative error also controls almost identical strings. On equal strings the successful output must be zero; an additive error term increasing with n would violate the statement. This requirement separates the question from weaker large-distance guarantees. The three cards therefore record distinct accuracy–runtime requirements, with their implications stated separately.
cards.why: Determine whether worst-case sequence alignment can simultaneously achieve arbitrarily small fixed relative error and a time exponent approaching one.

importance.reason: A central accuracy–runtime frontier for sequence comparison, with recent work on each side of the tradeoff. It is a genuinely stronger near-exact runtime target than TCS-7220, retained under the user’s explicit acceptance of related edit-distance questions.

progress.text: Andoni–Nosatzki establish constant-factor approximation in n^(1+η) time for every fixed η>0.

cards.title: Is distinguishing 3-colourable graphs from graphs needing more than six colours NP-hard?
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction R from Boolean 3-SAT to finite simple undirected graphs such that, for every 3-CNF formula F, satisfiability of F implies χ(R(F))≤3 and unsatisfiability of F implies χ(R(F))>6?
cards.definitions: A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses containing at most three literals, each literal being a Boolean variable or its negation; the formula and variable indices have a standard explicit finite binary encoding. R is a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine that outputs a graph as a labelled vertex set {1,…,n} and a list of unordered pairs of distinct vertices, with no repeated edges. Its total running time and output length are bounded by one polynomial in the formula’s encoding length. A proper k-colouring assigns one of {1,…,k} to each vertex so that endpoints of every edge receive different colours. χ(G) is the least such k, with χ of the empty graph taken to be zero. The promise decision problem, also denoted PCSP(K₃,K₆), has yes-instances χ≤3 and no-instances χ>6; graphs with χ=4,5,6 are outside the promise. K_k is the loopless complete graph on k vertices. No colouring or satisfiability witness is supplied as input. The reduction must satisfy the two implications unconditionally, without a Unique Games or Label Cover hardness hypothesis. Because 3-SAT is NP-complete, this reduction is precisely the usual deterministic many-one NP-hardness target for the promise problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
cards.context:
The input promise says that three colours suffice, but it does not reveal the three colour classes. Allowing a larger palette relaxes the output condition. The associated gap decision task distinguishes such promised yes-instances from graphs that cannot be coloured even with six colours. This isolates a small finite-template promise CSP with a particularly clear combinatorial meaning.

Barto, Bulín, Krokhin and Opršal establish hardness for colouring k-colourable graphs with 2k−1 colours, including the 3-versus-5 case. The 3-versus-6 question remains explicitly posed in subsequent work. Increasing the permitted palette weakens the output requirement, so hardness at five colours does not imply hardness at six.

TCS-6637 asks whether some fixed constant C admits a polynomial-time colouring algorithm for every 3-colourable graph. A negative result for six colours alone does not exclude algorithms using seven, one hundred or another fixed palette. Conversely, an algorithm with a growing number of colours does not settle even the six-colour search problem. The new card is a precise frontier case, rather than a duplicate of the quantifier over arbitrary constants.

The decision and search tasks should also be kept distinct. A polynomial-time six-colouring algorithm on 3-colourable inputs would decide the gap by checking its output: on a graph requiring more than six colours, no valid output exists. This implication explains the algorithmic relevance of the decision hardness target without redefining NP-hardness as a blanket statement about every search reduction.

The six-colour case has value beyond its small numerical parameters. It tests how far promise relaxation can preserve intractability after the classical CSP dichotomy, and it provides a fixed finite object on which algebraic and combinatorial limitations can be stated. Its specialist home remains Constraint satisfaction under the catalogue’s graph-category expansion.
cards.why: Resolve the next concrete constant-palette hardness case in approximate colouring and finite-template promise CSP.

importance.reason: A widely recognized frontier example for promise constraint satisfaction, explicitly posed beyond the known five-colour hardness. Kept separately from the all-constant algorithm question because it asks for an individually significant fixed-template reduction.

cards.title: Are first-order spectra closed under complementation?
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: For every first-order sentence φ over a finite relational vocabulary, does there exist a first-order sentence ψ over some finite relational vocabulary such that, for every positive integer n, ψ has a model with exactly n elements if and only if φ has no model with exactly n elements?
cards.definitions: A vocabulary is a finite list of relation symbols, each with a specified positive integer arity; the list and the arities may vary with the sentence and are not bounded by a fixed global constant. Equality is allowed. Sentences use variables, relation atoms, equality, Boolean connectives and first-order quantification, with no free variables. A finite model has a nonempty domain A and interprets each k-ary relation as a subset of A^k, with equality interpreted as equality on A. The spectrum Spec(φ) is {n∈N:n≥1 and some finite model of φ has cardinality n}. The required equality is Spec(ψ)=N_{>0} minus Spec(φ). The vocabulary of ψ need not be the vocabulary of φ. No bound on the length of ψ and no effective transformation φ↦ψ are required. Restricting to relational vocabularies loses no ordinary first-order spectra: functions and constants can be represented by their graph relations with first-order axioms for totality and uniqueness. This is closure of the class of spectra, not a decision procedure for finite satisfiability.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
cards.context:
A spectrum forgets the internal structure of a model and remembers only its possible finite sizes. A sentence can impose substantial combinatorial conditions on its relations, but the resulting object is just a subset of the positive integers. Asser’s question asks whether sizes excluded by one finite description can themselves be the allowed sizes of another finite description.

Negating the sentence does not solve the problem. If φ describes a graph consisting of disjoint edges covering all vertices, its spectrum contains the positive even numbers. An even-sized edgeless graph nevertheless satisfies ¬φ, so even numbers also belong to Spec(¬φ). Existence of a countermodel at a given size is different from absence of every model at that size.

The quantifier order is therefore essential. The target permits a new sentence ψ, chosen after φ but before n, which represents the entire complement simultaneously. It is not enough to provide a separate sentence for each excluded size. Allowing ψ a different vocabulary also prevents an arbitrary choice of representation from imposing an unintended extra restriction.

The spectrum problem helped shape finite model theory and descriptive complexity. The survey by Durand, Jones, Makowsky and More records Asser’s complement question as unresolved and connects the subject with bounded computational resources and structural restrictions on models. The importance here is the closure operation on the full expressive class, rather than one particular encoding of a graph family.

The existing logic-for-PTIME card asks for a logical characterization of efficient properties of individual finite structures. This card instead concerns the sets of cardinalities admitting some structure satisfying a sentence. It adds a different foundational question to the database and finite-model-theory bucket, even though both connect logic with computation.
cards.why: Determine a basic closure property of finite first-order expressibility after taking possible model sizes.

importance.reason: A classical foundational question of finite model theory and descriptive complexity, explicitly surveyed as an unresolved central spectrum problem. Its complement target is distinct from PTIME capture, query containment and ordinary finite satisfiability.

progress.text: Asser formulates whether complements of spectra are spectra, as documented in the historical survey.
The comprehensive survey retains the general complement question among its unresolved problems.

context_blocks.text: A spectrum forgets the internal structure of a model and remembers only its possible finite sizes. A sentence can impose substantial combinatorial conditions on its relations, but the resulting object is just a subset of the positive integers. Asser’s question asks whether sizes excluded by one finite description can themselves be the allowed sizes of another finite description.

Negating the sentence does not solve the problem. If φ describes a graph consisting of disjoint edges covering all vertices, its spectrum contains the positive even numbers. An even-sized edgeless graph nevertheless satisfies ¬φ, so even numbers also belong to Spec(¬φ). Existence of a countermodel at a given size is different from absence of every model at that size.

The quantifier order is therefore essential. The target permits a new sentence ψ, chosen after φ but before n, which represents the entire complement simultaneously. It is not enough to provide a separate sentence for each excluded size. Allowing ψ a different vocabulary also prevents an arbitrary choice of representation from imposing an unintended extra restriction.

The spectrum problem helped shape finite model theory and descriptive complexity. The survey by Durand, Jones, Makowsky and More records Asser’s complement question as unresolved and connects the subject with bounded computational resources and structural restrictions on models. The importance here is the closure operation on the full expressive class, rather than one particular encoding of a graph family.

The existing logic-for-PTIME card asks for a logical characterization of efficient properties of individual finite structures. This card instead concerns the sets of cardinalities admitting some structure satisfying a sentence. It adds a different foundational question to the database and finite-model-theory bucket, even though both connect logic with computation.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

New searches prioritize areas underrepresented relative to the last five completed STOC and FOCS editions. Conference shares guide collection; paper counts and open-problem counts are different quantities.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large groups of 50 and 24 named small groups of 20: 980 planned places are assigned to named categories and 20 places are reserved for future categories. These are future targets. Preliminary editorial pruning is recorded in the individual review manifests under to_delete/; final quota selection and a complete deduplication audit have not been performed. Topic assignments use original subjects, saved questions and primary source titles. Unclear cases go to Miscellaneous. General combinatorics outside the accepted scope is archived with a reason. Preliminary removals retain their reason and pre-removal selection category separately from original subject labels. Archived records remain accessible through the Selection scope filter and full exports. Original categories and stable IDs are preserved. Classification does not verify the statement or its current open status.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. Top 100 and Top 1000 use the first 5/2 and 50/20 category places respectively. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries. This is a review of importance and topical diversity, not a fresh verification of open status or completion of draft formulations. Importance scores are preserved.
